newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean loses another military leader in new blow.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean loses another military leader in new blow.

text.p: North Korea's vice defence minister died on Thursday, North Korean media reported, just days after the demise of the defence minister and other leadership upheavals.

Analysts said the death of Kim Kwang-jin -- he was reported to have been ill -- was a fresh blow to the nation's 1.1 million strong armed forces, still widely feared as the greatest threat to peace in Asia.
It injected new uncertainties into the communist nation, which is grappling with a sensitive political succession, destabilising food shortages and, possibly, a power struggle, they said.
Kim, the first vice-minister of the North Korean People's Armed Forces, died aged 69 of "incurable sickness", Pyongyang radio reported.
His superior, Choe Kwang, died of a heart attack last Friday, North Korean official media announced.

In quick succession, North Korea has lost two of the most powerful figures in a military hierachy that has a key role to play in the formal ascension to power of Kim Jong-il, son of "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, who died in 1994.
"For the armed forces, the death of the two top officials is a serious blow," said Noriyuki Suzuki, North Korean analyst at Japan's Radiopress news agency.
"This would inevitably force Kim Jong-il to speed up the process of generational change in the armed forces leadership."
Kim Jong-il needs military backing as he prepares to inherit the vacant titles of state president and general secretary of the Workers' Party.
Many North Korea watchers believe he will complete the socialist world's first dynastic succession after the third anniversary of his father's death in July.
Earlier this month, North Korea's Prime Minister was replaced -- apparently for health reasons -- and its chief ideologue defected to a South Korean diplomatic mission in Beijing.
The defection of Hwang Jang-yop dramatically revealed wavering loyalty at the top echelons of power to a political creed that has led to near-famine and economic ruin.
Hwang is still holed up at Seoul's consular office in the Chinese capital after arriving there by taxi with an aide on February 12.
South Korean efforts to persuade China to allow Hwang safe passage to Seoul have so far yielded no progress.
Kim Kwang-jin was also a member of the Central Committee of the ruling Workers' Party.
A state funeral will be held on Saturday, according to the Pyongyang radio report.
"At first sight the death of the No. 2 man in the North Korean armed forces might look very suspicious, coming only a week after the death of the No. 1," said Suzuki.

"But Kim Kwang-jin was seldom seen since last year and it looks as though his illness was genuine. His whereabouts were not known for much of last year and he was last reported to have taken part in a rally on January 3," he said.
"In fact the death of Choe is much more suspicious because he was reported to have attended birthday events for Kim Jong-il just five days before his death."
The line-up of Choe's funeral committee -- a fairly reliable gauge of power -- indicated the recent departure of senior figures was just the latest in a series of exits among the ruling elite.
Significant changes since a similar list was revealed two years ago fuelled speculation among the media and North Korea watchers of a power struggle.
